title: Cuadra traces Mexico’s growth constraints to productivity, investment and labour supply
summary: Deputy Governor José Gabriel Cuadra García uses a long-run growth accounting exercise to explain why Mexican output has grown slowly despite gains in labour, skills and capital. Between 1990 and 2019 real GDP growth averaged 2.3% in the decomposition. The contribution attributed to total factor productivity was negative over the period, with a particularly large drag in the 2000s. This accounting identifies how much recorded output growth remains after the measured inputs are taken into account. It does not identify a single cause of weak productivity. Cuadra presents his own analysis of Mexico’s growth prospects, with no new monetary-policy decision or forecast for the next meeting (pages 1–5).

The labour contribution could change as the population ages. Page 6 projects a rising ratio of people aged 65 and over to those aged 15–64. That measure counts people of working age regardless of whether they work. The distinction matters because the historical series on page 7 shows a sizable gap between male and female labour-force participation. The international comparison on page 8 places Mexico alongside Latin American and Caribbean economies. Some country observations predate the stated 2025 reference year, as the chart footnote explains. The evidence points to the importance of participation for future labour supply but supplies no estimate of how many additional people a particular policy would bring into employment.

Investment also responds unevenly to uncertainty. Page 13 models a one-standard-deviation increase in Mexican economic policy uncertainty using monthly data from 2001 to 2025. The two panels use the same normalization, scaling responses to a maximum decline of 1% in the activity measure. The central estimate for machinery and equipment falls further than the response of construction, and both estimated effects fade with time. The shaded bands show why the plotted troughs should be read as estimates. The adjacent charts distinguish residential from non-residential construction and private from public investment. A fall in aggregate investment can therefore conceal materially different changes in the purchases that build future productive capacity (pages 9–17).

Cuadra then moves from national productivity to differences among industries and the potential for new technologies to spread. The industry comparison on page 20 separates the top and bottom quarters of industries by productivity. Turning to artificial intelligence, the establishment survey on page 21 reports national use of 48.5% in June 2026 and prospective use of 64.8% over the following three years. It covers establishments with more than 100 workers. The September 2025 and June 2026 questions used different wording and horizons. A literal comparison of the two survey bars could therefore mix adoption with a change in the way respondents were asked about it.

Respondents also distinguish staff numbers from sales or gross revenue per worker. The stacks on page 22 separate past experience from expected effects, and responses depend on whether an establishment uses or expects to use at least one technology. Page 23 identifies security and privacy concerns, doubts about benefits, and shortages of qualified staff among reasons companies give for having no adoption plans. An additional chart on page 28 breaks use down by application. These responses describe managers’ perceptions and intentions. An aggregate productivity effect would require evidence on realized output, labour and capital across adopters and other firms. Cuadra closes the main chart sequence with pension assets, bank capital and private credit relative to GDP, putting the financing side of capital accumulation alongside the labour and technology evidence (pages 24–26).

questions.question: What explains the gap in productivity between the best- and worst-performing industries?
questions.detail: The growth accounting residual is negative over 1990–2019, and the industry breakdown shows that sectors followed markedly different paths. Neither identifies how much came from productivity changes within firms or the movement of resources across them. Decompose the same industry series using employment and capital weights and examine firm entry and exit. That separation would help locate potential sources of a durable change in growth.

questions.question: Can reported AI adoption be linked to measured gains in output per worker?
questions.detail: The June survey covers larger establishments and distinguishes use today from plans over three years. Managers can report higher expected sales per worker before any gain has materialized. Match respondents to subsequent output, prices, hours and capital spending and compare adopters with similar establishments that had not adopted. Keeping definitions and survey wording constant would help distinguish adoption from a change in measurement.

questions.question: Which investment categories bear the largest lasting loss after an uncertainty shock?
questions.detail: The model displays a deeper initial decline for machinery than construction, while separate charts reveal heterogeneity within both categories. For an assessment of future productive capacity, examine whether firms subsequently make up deferred equipment purchases. Compare several shock definitions and vintages of investment data, retaining the published output normalization so that differing scales do not create spurious differences in the estimated effects.
